**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the Temple as the official centre of Jewish worship and a centre for unity in Palestine

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Temple at Jerusalem, rebuilt and enlarged by Herod the Great, stood at the heart of Jewish religious life in the time of Jesus. To examine it critically means to weigh the ways in which it did unite the Jews, and the ways in which it also exposed their divisions. The answer is that the Temple was indeed the official centre of worship and a powerful symbol of unity, but that its unity was partial and was weakened by politics, wealth and rival groups.

**1. The Temple as the official centre of worship.**
- It was the only place where the sacrifices commanded in the Law could be offered. The daily morning and evening offerings were made there on behalf of the whole nation.
- The priests and Levites served there, and the high priest alone entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement.
- The great pilgrim feasts of Passover, Pentecost (Weeks) and Tabernacles brought Jews to Jerusalem from all over Palestine. Luke shows this when the boy Jesus goes up to Jerusalem with his family for the Passover (Luke 2:41-42).
- The Temple tax paid by Jewish men supported the services, and the Sanhedrin met in the Temple area.
- Luke begins and ends his Gospel in the Temple: Zechariah is serving there when the angel appears (Luke 1:8-11), Jesus is presented there (Luke 2:22-38), and the disciples are found blessing God in the Temple at the end (Luke 24:53).

**2. The Temple as a centre of unity.**
- There was one God and one Temple, which gave Jews a shared identity and a common place of prayer, whether they lived in Galilee, Judaea or the Dispersion.
- Jews of the Dispersion sent gifts and pilgrims, and so the Temple linked Palestine with the Jews scattered abroad.
- The Court of the Gentiles also made room for non-Jews who feared God, which gave the Temple a wider role in Jewish thought.

**3. Critical points: the limits of that unity.**
- The Temple was controlled by a wealthy priestly aristocracy, chiefly Sadducees, appointed and watched by the Roman authorities. Many ordinary Jews resented its wealth and its cooperation with Rome.
- The Pharisees stressed the Law and the synagogue and the Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim and rejected Jerusalem (compare John 4:20). Some groups, such as the Qumran community, rejected the Temple priesthood altogether.
- Jesus himself criticised abuses when he drove out the traders (Luke 19:45-46) and foretold the destruction of the Temple (Luke 21:5-6). The Temple was in fact destroyed by the Romans in AD 70.

**Conclusion.** The Temple was undoubtedly the official centre of Jewish worship and the strongest symbol of national unity. Yet the unity it provided was religious rather than political, and it was strained by the rival sects, by Roman control and by abuse. It is therefore better described as a powerful but contested centre.
